topics.name: Solid Waste

rows.t: 62 million t a year generated, 43 collected, only 12 treated (TERI) → 165 million t by 2030
rules not implemented + no political will + no designated sites → open dumps and legacy landfills (≈8.8 crore t legacy waste, Ghazipur fires)
no <mark>segregation at source</mark> + low door-to-door collection
overconsumption + FMCG packaging: consumption grew, collection didn't + too few processing units: only 15–20% processed
low municipal finance (poor creditworthiness)
overlapping jurisdiction between agencies
Health: landfill fires and disease near dumps
Environment: leachate into groundwater + methane from landfills
Economy: materials worth crores lost instead of recycled
Society: waste pickers work unprotected
one dedicated, enforced rulebook <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">SWM Rules 2026</button>
GPS-tracked door-to-door collection (Bhopal) + waste processors at scale (Mumbai, Bhopal)
designated sites + biomine legacy dumps (DRAP) + yearly landfill audits
segregation at source: <mark>Indore</mark> (best example) + Anupam Colony, Delhi + SWaCH, Pune
cut waste at source, treat it as a resource <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">Circular economy</button>
user fees + waste cess (Bengaluru proposal) + Garbage Free City star rating
Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0 + clear roles for ULBs

hs.b:
• From 1 Apr 2026, replaced the 2016 Rules: 3-way → 4-stream segregation
  • Bulk generators process their wet waste or buy an EBWGR certificate + refuse-derived fuel to cement plants
  • Yearly landfill audits + tourist user fee in hills and islands + polluter-pays compensation
  • Also: C&D Waste Rules, 2025 + Contaminated Sites Rules 2025

• Only 7.2% of the world economy is circular (9.1% in 2018) + India could be a $2 trillion market with 1 crore jobs by 2050
  • Waste to wealth: biogas from wet waste + gasification, pyrolysis + GOBARdhan plants · Indore: Asia's largest Bio-CNG plant (2022)
  • India: Mission LiFE + EPR rules + Steel Scrap Recycling Policy + NITI Circular Economy Cell
  • Gaps: downcycling + informal sector recovers only 10–20% of materials + fake EPR certificates
  • Fix: EPR across sectors (plastic, e-waste, batteries, tyres) + recycled-content mandates + design for reuse · Mixed: Alang ship recycling (Hong Kong Convention in force 2025)

cm.0: Leachate = the toxic liquid that drains out of rotting garbage and seeps into groundwater.
cm.1: EBWGR = Extended Bulk Waste Generator Responsibility: big generators (malls, hotels) that don't process their wet waste must buy certificates from those who do.
cm.2: Refuse-derived fuel (RDF) = dry burnable waste (plastic, paper) shredded into fuel for cement kilns instead of coal.
cm.3: C&D Waste Rules 2025 (in force 1 Apr 2026, replace the 2016 rules): builders answer for their debris (EPR) + recycling targets + 5% recycled material in construction from 2026–27, rising to 25% by 2030–31.
cm.4: Biomining = digging up old dumps, sieving the waste and recovering soil, recyclables and fuel. Legacy waste = waste dumped years ago that never got treated.
cm.5: DRAP = Dumpsite Remediation Accelerator Programme (SBM-Urban 2.0) to clear old landfills fast.
cm.6: Steel Scrap Recycling Policy (2019): framework for organised scrapping centres, so old vehicles and goods become scrap for steel-making instead of imported scrap.
cm.7: Downcycling = recycling into a lower-value product each time (a bottle becomes a mat), so the material is eventually lost.
cm.8: Alang, Gujarat = world's largest ship-breaking yard. Hong Kong Convention (IMO, in force June 2025) = safe, clean ship recycling rules.

topics.name: E-Waste

rows.t: India is 3rd largest after the USA and China: ≈6 million t (2024) → 14 million t by 2030 + only 10% formally recycled (world ≈22%)
fake recyclers distort the EPR market + EPR covers only gold, copper, iron, aluminium
crude methods: circuit boards stripped with acid
low awareness, old devices go to kabadiwalas
85% handled by the informal sector
80% of rich countries' e-waste is shipped to developing countries
Health and environment: lead, mercury, cadmium leach into groundwater (Moradabad: Ramganga mercury 8x the standard, CSE 2015)
Economy: ₹51,000 crore of materials lost (Paryavaran NITI Manthan)
widen and police EPR <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">E-waste rules</button>
hydrometallurgy + AI-based recovery + bioleaching (microbes pull metals out of waste)
Kerala's Haritha Karma Sena buys e-waste door to door at fixed rates (2025)
train and certify informal workers
GST-linked checks on recyclers + a recycling wing in the National Critical Mineral Mission
global rules on dumping <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">Basel + Stockholm</button>

hs.b:
• 2011: EPR introduced (producer cleans what he produces) → 2016: Producer Responsibility Organisations
  • 2022: CPCB portal + tradable EPR certificates bought from registered recyclers + items covered 21 → 106
  • Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022

• Basel Convention (1989): controls transboundary movement of hazardous waste, stops rich countries dumping e-waste on poor ones
  • Stockholm Convention (2001): eliminates persistent organic pollutants (the "Dirty Dozen", e.g. DDT)

cm.0: Battery Waste Management Rules 2022: EPR for battery makers (collect and recycle all batteries, incl. EV) + minimum recycled content in new batteries + tradable EPR certificates.
cm.1: Bioleaching = using microbes to pull metals out of e-waste. Hydrometallurgy = dissolving metals out with chemicals instead of burning.
cm.2: National Critical Mineral Mission (2025, ₹16,300 crore): find, mine and process critical minerals (lithium, cobalt, rare earths) at home and abroad + incentives to recover them from e-waste and old batteries.

topics.name: Hazardous & Biomedical Waste

rows.t: hazardous = toxic, flammable, reactive or corrosive + biomedical ≈609 t a day (+101 t a day in COVID)
small clinics hard to monitor + illegal imports
poor segregation in hospitals + informal recyclers without safety gear + people oppose new TSDFs near them
industry, hospitals, coal plants, gold mining + few treatment, storage and disposal facilities (TSDFs) + few common biomedical facilities (CBWTFs) in rural areas
Health: Bhopal: 337 t of Union Carbide toxic waste burnt at Pithampur only in 2025, 40 years later
Environment: toxins leach into soil and groundwater
enforce the 2016 rules <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">Waste rules 2016</button>
clean old toxic sites with bioremediation and phytoremediation + Contaminated Sites Rules 2025 (189 substances)
IMAGE, Palakkad: doctors' association runs one common biomedical facility for Kerala's private hospitals
cleaner production + formalise informal recyclers + more TSDFs and CBWTFs, especially rural

hs.b:
• Methylmercury is the most toxic form: bioaccumulates in fish, harms foetuses and children
  • Failed: Minamata, Japan (1956, factory waste) + Kodaikanal, Tamil Nadu (2001, HUL thermometer factory)
  • India: ratified the Minamata Convention (2018) + mercury limits for coal plants (2015) + mercury thermometers out of hospitals
  • Gap: coal plants slow on controls (≈78% of Category C plants exempted from FGD, Jul 2025)

• Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016 (under EPA): SPCB authorisation for generators + duties for TSDF operators
  • Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016 (amended 2018, 2019): colour-coded bins + common facilities (CBWTFs) + incineration, autoclave, microwave + secured landfill

cm.0: TSDF = Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility for hazardous waste. CBWTF = Common Bio-medical Waste Treatment Facility shared by hospitals.
cm.1: Methylmercury = the form mercury takes in water and fish; it builds up the food chain and damages the brain.
cm.2: FGD = flue gas desulphurisation: scrubbers that remove SO₂ from power-plant smoke. Category C plants = those far from big cities and polluted areas.
cm.3: Contaminated Sites Rules 2025 = rules to find, list and clean up old toxic sites, with the polluter paying.

pyq: 2014 Q15 (12.5 marks): Environmental Impact Assessment studies are increasingly undertaken before a project is cleared by the Government. Discuss the environmental impacts of coal-fired thermal plants located at coal pitheads.

rows.t: fall in land's biological or economic productivity (UNCCD); in drylands = desertification + India ≈30% of land degraded (ISRO Atlas), Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Jharkhand worst
policies reward over-irrigation and fertiliser (Punjab–Haryana canals → waterlogging, salinity)
water erosion (biggest) + wind erosion (Thar) + invasive Lantana in ≈50% of forest and scrubland (SOE 2026)
overgrazing + shifting cultivation
deforestation + mining
Environment: soils are the 2nd largest carbon pool after oceans (2,500 Gt) + dust storms + silted reservoirs + India breached the land-system-change boundary (SOE 2026)
Economy: lower yields
Society: rural distress and migration (affects 3.2 billion people worldwide)
LDN target: restore 26 million ha by 2030 (≈24 million ha done or under way)
ISRO Desertification Atlas + Soil Health Card

watershed development (PMKSY-WDC) + afforestation (Green India Mission, Aravalli Green Wall) + restore whole landscapes, not just plant trees · Ralegan Siddhi (watershed revived groundwater and farms)
grazing control + local techniques (Zai pits) + land tenure rights for local communities
change how we farm <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">Natural farming</button><button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">Agroforestry</button>
: Green Credit Programme

hs.b:
• Bonn Challenge: restore 350 million ha worldwide by 2030 (India pledged 26 million ha)
  • UNCCD COP16, Riyadh 2024: Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership ($12 billion+) + land tenure for local communities
  • UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030)

• Chemical-free farming with on-farm inputs (organic buys inputs from outside; natural doesn't)
  • Pillars: Beejamrit + Jeevamrit + mulching + Whapasa
  • Worked: Andhra Pradesh APCNF (lakhs of farmers, lower input costs) · Failed: Sri Lanka 2021 (overnight fertiliser ban → yields crashed)
  • India: National Mission on Natural Farming (2024, ₹2,481 crore, 1 crore farmers)
  • Gaps: yields may dip in early years + needs cattle for inputs + few premium markets → fix: phased shift (Sri Lanka lesson) + certification + market links

• Trees with crops or livestock on farms: ≈8.5% of land + National Agroforestry Policy 2014 (India first in the world)
  • Gains: crop yields up ≈50% + stores 14–27 t CO₂ per ha a year (EAC-PM) + half of fuelwood, 60% of paper-pulp wood
  • Worked: poplar on farm bunds, Punjab–Haryana (feeds the plywood industry)
  • India: Trees Outside Forests in India (2023) + SMAF (under NMSA) + NITI's GROW initiative
  • Gap: felling and transit permits → adopt model felling rules in every state

cm.0: SOE = State of India's Environment report (CSE). Land-system change = one of 9 planetary boundaries: how much forest and natural land can be converted before Earth systems are pushed out of a safe zone.
cm.1: LDN = Land Degradation Neutrality: restore as much land as is degraded, so net damage is zero.
cm.2: PMKSY-WDC = the watershed part of Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana: rainwater harvesting and soil conservation on a whole catchment.
cm.3: Zai pits = small planting pits that trap rain and compost, from the Sahel; they revive dry, hard soil.
cm.4: Beejamrit = seed treatment with cow dung and urine; Jeevamrit = fermented dung-urine mix that feeds soil microbes; Whapasa = soil with both air and moisture in it.
cm.5: APCNF = Andhra Pradesh Community-managed Natural Farming: the largest natural farming programme in India.
cm.6: Trees Outside Forests in India = MoEFCC + USAID programme (2023) to grow trees on farms and private land. SMAF = Sub-Mission on Agroforestry (under the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture). GROW = NITI Aayog's Greening and Restoration of Wasteland with Agroforestry (maps wasteland fit for agroforestry).
cm.7: Green Credit Programme = earn tradable credits for tree planting, water saving and other green actions.

topics.name: Energy Transition

rows.t: non-fossil = 50% of installed capacity, reached June 2025 (2030 NDC target, 5 years early) + 250 GW RE, 3rd in the world + but under 30% of generation (capacity ≠ generation) + WEF Energy Transition Index 2024: 71 of 118
Health: cleaner air (capability approach by amartya sen)(removes a major unfreedom )
Environment: cuts CO₂, the road to net zero 2070
Economy: oil and coal import cut + 1.3 million RE jobs (7.7% of world), 2nd in solar PV jobs after China (IRENA 2025)
Governance: energy security (West Asia crisis)
Society: energy access: decentralised RE empowers communities (Barefoot Women Solar Engineers)
fossil fuels still get ≈5x the subsidy of clean energy (IISD, FY24) <button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">Subsidy shift</button>
storage costly (≈₹5–6 per unit) + lag in latest solar cells
RE cant provide energy 24x7 as solar during day time and wind during blowing winds (no BESS) + spread thin: solar needs 300x the land of nuclear
farmers and herders lose land and grazing commons (orans) without consent → protests + coal workers face job loss (150+ districts live off coal and thermal power)
≈80% of solar modules from China + power lines in the Thar kill Great Indian Bustards <button class="hs chipx" data-h="3">GIB conflict</button>
$6.5 trillion needed by 2070 for net zero + DISCOM debt + stranded coal assets
weak transmission, states slow on intra-state lines <button class="hs chipx" data-h="4">Green Energy Corridor</button>
shift subsidies from fossil to clean + Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022
storage (ACC battery PLI, pumped storage) + smart grids + new sources: geothermal (first policy 2025, 381 hot springs), CO₂-to-methanol (NTPC Vindhyachal), coal gasification (100 MT by 2030)
wind-solar hybrids + one cross-border grid (OSOWOG)
decentralised RE: rooftops (PM Surya Ghar) + farms (PM-KUSUM) (will cause habitual energy storage of solar energy)
domestic manufacturing (PLI) + a just transition for coal regions
JETP + green bonds + blended finance
independent national body for coal phase-out + Green Energy Corridor Phases 3 and 4

hs.b:
• Capacity: 50% non-fossil reached June 2025, 5 years early → next 60% by 2035
  • Generation by using RE is still under 30% + coal still ≈55% of energy needs
  • Verdict: the capacity target is met; 50% of energy needs only with storage, grid and green hydrogen

• SDG 7: affordable, reliable, sustainable, modern energy for all
  • UJALA (2015): 36.87 crore LED bulbs distributed, saving ₹19,153 crore a year (PIB 2025) (new)
  • LEDs use 90% less power than old bulbs, 50% less than CFLs → ≈48 billion units saved a year, ≈9,500 MW peak demand avoided (new, PIB)

• Fossil support fell to 5x clean energy in FY24, the smallest gap in 5 years; clean subsidies up 31% to ≈₹32,000 crore (IISD 2025) (new)
  • But 83% of new PSU investment still goes to fossil assets (IISD)
  • How the shift helps: frees money for storage and grid + makes RE cheaper than coal + steady signal to investors
  • Use fossil tax revenue to fund clean energy (IISD) (new)

• Thar and Kutch: power lines kill Great Indian Bustards (under 150 left)
  • SC 2021 ordered lines underground, eased 2024

• Lines that carry solar and wind power from RE-rich states into the grid + Renewable Energy Management Centres; work began 2015 (new, Ministry of Power)
  • Phase I: inter-state part done (Mar 2020); intra-state part in 8 states delayed by right-of-way and GIB court cases
  • Phase II: 7 states, ≈10,750 km of lines, ≈₹12,000 crore, 33% central aid + Ladakh 13 GW line (2024)
  • Next: Phases 3 and 4 to cover the whole country (new, DTE)

• Mining companies pay 10% or 30% of royalty into District Mineral Foundations; ≥70% to health, water, education, women and child welfare
  • Mixed: Keonjhar, Odisha (huge fund, spent on roads and buildings) · Worked: Dantewada (education, livelihoods)
  • Problems: large unspent balances + Collector-run trusts, little Gram Sabha say
  • Fix: real Gram Sabha role + social audits (revised guidelines 2024)

cm.0: Capacity vs generation: capacity = how much power plants could make at full tilt; generation = what they actually make. Solar runs only in daylight, so 50% of capacity gives far less than 50% of electricity.
cm.1: WEF Energy Transition Index = World Economic Forum ranking of how ready countries are to move to clean energy.
cm.2: Barefoot Women Solar Engineers = rural women trained (Barefoot College, Tilonia) to install and fix solar lights in their villages.
cm.3: SDG 7 = UN goal of affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all by 2030.
cm.4: CFL = compact fluorescent lamp, the curly tube bulb that came before LEDs.
cm.5: BESS = Battery Energy Storage System: big battery banks that store solar or wind power and release it when needed (at night, at peak).
cm.6: DISCOM = state power distribution company that buys power and sells it to homes; most are in debt, so they pay generators late.
cm.7: Stranded assets = coal plants and mines that become unprofitable before they're paid off because cheaper clean power takes over.
cm.8: Renewable Energy Management Centres = control rooms that forecast solar and wind output and balance the grid in real time.
cm.9: Green Energy Open Access = big consumers (100 kW+) can buy green power directly from any producer instead of only their DISCOM. Status: Karnataka HC struck the central Rules down in Jan 2025 (only state commissions can make open-access rules) → states now notify their own green open access regulations (Haryana, Rajasthan 2025; Delhi 2026).
cm.10: ACC = Advanced Chemistry Cell (lithium-ion and newer batteries); PLI = Production Linked Incentive, cash rewards for making them in India. Pumped storage = pump water uphill when power is spare, release it through turbines when needed: a giant water battery.
cm.11: Methanol = a liquid fuel made from coal, gas or captured CO₂; it can be blended in petrol or used in ships.
cm.12: Coal gasification = turning coal into gas (syngas) for fuels and chemicals instead of burning it, so pollutants are easier to capture.
cm.13: OSOWOG = One Sun One World One Grid: link solar grids across countries so the sun is always shining somewhere. GGI = Green Grids Initiative, its launch platform.
cm.14: PLI = Production Linked Incentive: the government pays makers a share of their extra sales for 4–6 years, to build factories in India (solar modules, batteries, electrolysers).
cm.15: PMKKKY = Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (2015): spends District Mineral Foundation money on the people and areas hit by mining.
cm.16: JETP = Just Energy Transition Partnership: rich countries' finance package to help a country move off coal (South Africa, Indonesia, Vietnam). Green bonds = loans raised from investors only for green projects.

topics.name: Solar

rows.t: 150 GW (Mar 2026), 3rd in the world (Rajasthan, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu top) + potential ≈3,343 GW, rooftop alone 750 GW + ≈300 sunny days a year
Benefits: no fuel to import + no emissions + sits on rooftops and farms + fastest to build
Examples: Bhadla, Rajasthan (≈2.2 GW on desert land) + Modhera, Gujarat (first 24x7 solar village, 2022)
lag in latest cells (PERC, bifacial, thin-film)
no power after sunset → storage needed
households slow to put up rooftop panels (PM Surya Ghar target: 1 crore homes; upfront ₹40,000–70,000 per kW)
≈80% of modules from China (≈35 million imported in FY25) + mining for solar minerals scars land (Economic Survey 2023–24)
weak DISCOM finances
protect domestic makers <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">ALMM + PLI</button>
move to PERC and bifacial cells
one cross-border grid so the sun is always shining somewhere <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">GGI–OSOWOG</button>
solar for homes and farms <button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">PM Surya Ghar</button><button class="hs chipx" data-h="3">PM-KUSUM</button>
reverse auctions keep tariffs low → now cheaper than coal <button class="hs chipx" data-h="4">Solar cost fall</button>

hs.b:
• ALMM: only approved (mostly domestic) modules for government projects
  • PLI for solar PV + National Solar Mission, 2010 + Solar Park Scheme

• Launched by India + UK at COP26 (2 Nov 2021), run by ISA with the World Bank → round-the-clock clean power, less storage needed
  • First floated by the PM at ISA's First Assembly, Oct 2018
  • Phases: India linked to Middle East, South Asia, South-East Asia → African power pools → global grid
  • Backed by 80+ ISA members (One Sun Declaration)

• Rooftop solar + 300 free units a month
  • 1 crore families save ≈₹15,000 crore a year
• Solar pumps for farmers + grid-connected solar on barren land

• Why: Chinese mass production + better cells + reverse auctions + solar parks with ready land and lines (new)
  • For thermal plants: run fewer hours, old units become stranded assets, coal shifts to backup role (new)

cm.0: PERC = a cheaper, more efficient solar cell design; bifacial panels catch sunlight on both sides; thin-film = flexible, lightweight panels.
cm.1: ALMM = Approved List of Models and Manufacturers: only listed (mostly Indian) solar panels can be used in government-backed projects.
cm.2: National Solar Mission (2010): one of the 8 NAPCC missions; first target 20 GW of solar by 2022, raised to 100 GW in 2015.
cm.3: Solar Park = a big plot with ready land, roads and grid lines where developers plug in solar plants cheaply.
cm.4: ISA = International Solar Alliance: India–France-led group of sunny countries (launched at COP21, 2015) to spread solar power; HQ in Gurugram. One Sun Declaration (COP26) = 80+ countries backing the one-world-grid idea.
cm.5: Reverse auction = developers bid the lowest price per unit to win a project, which pushed solar tariffs down.

rows.t: ≈56 GW (2026; 21 GW in 2014), 4th in the world + offshore potential ≈36 GW off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu
Benefits: 70–80% of components made in India → less import dependence than solar
Example: Muppandal, Tamil Nadu (India's largest wind cluster)
big minimum project size
offshore turbines are noisy for marine life
land acquisition delays + power lines kill Great Indian Bustards (Thar, Kutch)
offshore costly (salt corrosion)
states slow on intra-state transmission lines
Green Open Access Rules 2022
repower old low-height turbines
wind-solar hybrids (Hybrid Policy 2018)
viability gap funding for offshore

hs.b:
• National Offshore Wind Energy Policy 2015 + offshore VGF
  • ≈36 GW potential off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu
  • India–UK offshore wind taskforce

cm.0: Big minimum project size = central auctions and direct grid connection need large utility-scale wind farms, typically 50 MW or more.
cm.1: Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022: any consumer with 100 kW+ load (earlier 1 MW) can buy wind or solar power directly from a producer through the grid, not only from its DISCOM. Why it matters: factories and offices can go green on their own → demand for wind and solar grows beyond government auctions and weak DISCOMs + no surcharges for green hydrogen + offshore wind waiver till 2032. Status: Karnataka HC struck the central Rules down (Jan 2025: only state commissions can make open-access rules) → states now make their own green open access regulations.
cm.2: Repowering = replacing old small wind turbines with taller, stronger ones on the same site to get more power.
cm.3: Wind-solar hybrid = wind and solar at the same site sharing one grid line; wind blows at night, sun in the day.
cm.4: VGF (viability gap funding) = a one-time government grant that covers the part of a project's cost the market won't pay.
cm.5: National Offshore Wind Energy Policy 2015: opens India's sea, up to 200 nautical miles (EEZ), to wind farms; NIWE, Chennai, is the nodal agency that allots blocks.

topics.name: Hydro

rows.t: hydro gives flexible power that balances solar and wind; pumped storage works as a giant battery <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">Run-of-river</button>
Barriers: N fragile Himalaya (Chamoli 2021 hit the Tapovan project; Sikkim 2023 broke the Chungthang dam) + C displacement and local protests
Fixes: minimum e-flow + careful siting + pumped storage for RE

hs.b:
• Uses the river's natural flow with little or no reservoir: water diverted through a tunnel to turbines, then returned downstream (new)
  • vs storage dam: a big reservoir stores water and generates on demand; run-of-river output rises and falls with river flow (new)
  • Pros: less submergence and displacement · Cons: dry stretch between intake and outlet + weak in the lean season (new)

cm.0: Run-of-river = a hydro plant that uses the river's natural flow without a big dam or reservoir.

pyq: 2013 Q17b (5 marks): What do you understand by Run-of-river hydroelectricity project? How is it different from any other hydroelectricity project?

topics.name: Nuclear

rows.t: 8.18 GW (Jan 2025) → 22.48 GW by 2031–32 → 100 GW by 2047 (Nuclear Energy Mission, Budget 2025–26)
Benefits: large thorium reserves + low pollution + little land + 24x7 power
Examples: Kudankulam (largest plant, Russian VVERs) · Jaitapur (planned since 2010, stuck on liability, cost, protests)
Three-stage programme <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">3-stage + FBR</button>
<button class="hs" data-h="1">Facts vs fears</button>
Fusion <button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">ITER</button>
liability law (CLNDA 2010) kept suppliers away now shanti act introduced
uranium shortfall + extraction needs sulphuric acid
locals not consulted → protests (Kudankulam)
high cost, long delays (PFBR ≈16 years late)
SHANTI Act + amendments to Atomic Energy Act 1962 and CLNDA 2010 for private participation
Bharat Small Reactors + at least 5 SMRs by 2033
put reactors on retiring coal-plant sites

hs.b:
• Stage 1: heavy-water reactors on natural uranium → plutonium · Stage 2: fast breeders burn plutonium (MOX) and breed more fuel than they use · Stage 3: thorium
  • PFBR, Kalpakkam (500 MWe, BHAVINI): first criticality 6 Apr 2026 → India enters stage 2 (new, PIB)
  • Advantage: unlocks India's thorium + fuel security
  • But: ≈16 years late, cost more than doubled (new)

• Facts: 24x7 low-carbon power + little land + thorium future
  • Fears: accidents (Fukushima 2011) + long-lived waste + liability + delays and cost (PFBR) + local protests (Jaitapur, Kudankulam)

• ITER, France: 7 members (EU, US, Russia, China, Japan, Korea, India); India's share ≈9%, given in kind (new)
  • India built the 3,850-tonne cryostat (its largest of 14 packages) + in-wall shielding, cooling water and cryogenic systems, diagnostics (new, ITER)
  • Domestic base: Aditya tokamak at the Institute for Plasma Research
  • If it works: near-limitless fuel from seawater, no long-lived waste, no meltdown risk, but commercial power is decades away

cm.0: Nuclear Energy Mission = Budget 2025–26 push for 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047, incl. small reactors and private players.
cm.1: VVER = Russian-design pressurised water reactor, used at Kudankulam.
cm.2: Heavy-water reactor (PHWR) = India's main reactor type, runs on natural uranium and uses heavy water to slow neutrons.
cm.3: MOX = mixed oxide fuel: uranium plus plutonium. Fast breeder = a reactor that makes more fuel than it burns.
cm.4: PFBR = Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor: India's first fast breeder (500 MWe) at Kalpakkam; makes more fuel than it burns.
cm.5: BHAVINI = Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam, the PSU that built and runs the Kalpakkam fast breeder.
cm.6: Cryostat = the giant steel vacuum shell that keeps ITER's magnets super-cold.
cm.7: Tokamak = a doughnut-shaped machine that holds super-hot plasma with magnets for fusion. Aditya = India's first, at IPR Gandhinagar.
cm.8: CLNDA = Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010: lets the operator sue suppliers after an accident, which scared foreign suppliers away.
cm.9: SHANTI Act = the new nuclear law opening the sector to private players and reworking the liability rules.
cm.10: Bharat Small Reactor = 220 MW Indian reactor for captive use by industry. SMR = small modular reactor, factory-built and easy to place.

rows.t: India uses ≈6.5 million t of hydrogen a year, mostly grey
Benefits: cleans hard-to-abate sectors (steel, cement, fertiliser, refineries) + energy security + 3x the energy of petrol per kg
Examples: Leh green-hydrogen buses (NTPC, 2023) + NTPC Kawas, Gujarat (hydrogen blended into piped gas, 2023) <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">Hydrogen colours</button>
storage and safety (flammable)
up to 9 litres of water per kg
most hydrogen still grey
$4–7 per kg, still costly
demand mandates for fertiliser and refineries <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">NGHM</button>
cheaper electrolysers (PLI)
green hydrogen hubs

hs.b:
• Grey: from natural gas, CO₂ released
  • Blue: from gas, CO₂ captured (CCUS); bridge fuel, cheaper now
  • Green: electrolysis of water with RE, zero carbon
  • Pink: electrolysis with nuclear power, 24x7 (BARC research)

• National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023): 5 million t of green hydrogen a year by 2030 + 1 lakh crore cut in fossil fuel imports + 50 MMT of GHG averted + 125 GW capacity will be added
  • SIGHT incentives + hydrogen hubs + certification scheme
  • Pilots: GAIL blending in CNG and PNG (Indore) + first hydrogen train coach (ICF) + Kandla port plant + Varanasi fuel-cell boat

cm.0: Hard-to-abate = heavy industries (steel, cement, fertiliser) whose emissions can't be cut easily just by switching to renewable power.
cm.1: Electrolysis = splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity.
cm.2: SIGHT = Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition: incentives for making electrolysers and green hydrogen in India.

topics.name: Bioenergy

rows.t: bioenergy ≈11.6 GW (Nov 2025) + waste-to-energy ≈0.85 GW + modern bioenergy = 13% of final energy use
Benefits: farm waste becomes energy + less stubble burning + farmer income (Annadata to Urjadata) + forex saved <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">Biofuel generations</button>
ethanol policy leans on cane and grain (1st gen) → food vs fuel
2G plants run well below capacity (Panipat 2G refinery)
cane is water-heavy → more blending = more cane = more water + biomass has competing uses (fodder, manure)
mixed wet waste burns poorly → waste-to-energy plants underrun + emissions near homes (Okhla, NGT fine 2017)
weak straw supply chain + no organised biomass market (fragmented human coordination—individual smallholders lack the labour, baling capacity, and market intermediaries to aggregate paddy straw.)
low private investment
blending mandates <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">E20 / EBP</button>
2G ethanol (PM JI-VAN) + online emission monitoring at waste-to-energy plants

villages run their own biogas from dung and farm waste (GOBARdhan) + segregation at source so waste-to-energy plants get only dry waste (SWM Rules 2026) + biomethanation for wet waste <button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">SATAT + GOBARdhan</button>
H: FPO-run biomass depots + national biomass repository + GIS maps of biomass + plants near the feedstock
viability gap funding <button class="hs chipx" data-h="3">Biotech role</button>

hs.b:
• 1st: edible crops (sugarcane, wheat, corn) → food vs fuel
  • 2nd: non-edible parts (straw, grass, wood)
  • 3rd: algae · 4th: waste to fuel (pyrolysis)

• EBP (2003) → E20 met in 2025, 5 years early; E20 mandatory with RON 95 from 1 Apr 2026
  • ₹1.84 lakh crore forex saved + ₹1.58 lakh crore to farmers + maize share 0% → 42%
  • Cane / maize ethanol cut GHG 65% / 50% vs petrol (NITI)
  • National Policy on Biofuels 2018 (rev. 2022): E20 by 2025 + 2G ethanol, biodiesel, bio-CNG + non-food feedstock
  • Support: Ethanol Interest Subvention + GST 18% → 5%
  • Concerns: food diverted + water-heavy cane + 3–7% lower mileage in older vehicles

• Lehragaga, Sangrur, Punjab: India's largest compressed biogas plant on paddy straw (SATAT, 2022)
  • Indore GOBARdhan: wet waste → Bio-CNG for city buses (2022)
  • National Bioenergy Programme (2022, ₹1,715 crore)

• Enzymes break straw into 2G ethanol + algae for 3rd-gen fuel + microbes for biogas and bio-CNG (new)
  • Turns waste into fuel → less oil import, the path to energy independence by 2047 (new)

cm.0: 2G ethanol = ethanol made from crop waste (straw, stalks) instead of food crops.
cm.1: EBP = Ethanol Blended Petrol programme; E20 = 20% ethanol in petrol.
cm.2: RON 95 = octane rating of petrol; higher octane needed for E20 to run smoothly in engines.
cm.3: PM JI-VAN = scheme giving viability gap funding to build 2G ethanol plants.
cm.4: Compressed biogas (CBG) = biogas cleaned and compressed to work like CNG in vehicles.
cm.5: SATAT = Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (2018): oil companies promise to buy compressed biogas from new plants that run on farm waste, dung and city waste.
cm.6: GOBARdhan = scheme turning cattle dung and farm waste into biogas and manure in villages.
cm.7: National Bioenergy Programme (MNRE, 2022–26): funds waste-to-energy, biomass (briquettes, pellets) and biogas plants.
cm.8: H = human collectives (FPOs running collection depots) with decision-support tools (GIS maps that show planners and FPOs where surplus biomass is).
cm.9: FPO = Farmer Producer Organisation: a farmers' company that can collect and sell straw in bulk.

Benefits: ≈3x less CO₂ even on today's grid + ≈60% energy efficiency vs ≈20% for petrol + 30% EVs by 2030 saves ≈₹1.1 lakh crore of oil imports a year
: inverted GST (18% on inputs, 5% on EVs)
battery minerals (lithium, cobalt) imported
e-buses and e-trucks cost 2–3x + public charging ≈4x the cost of home charging
battery recycling under EPR (2022 rules) + National Critical Mineral Mission for lithium
EVs as grid batteries <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">V2G</button>
subsidies for EVs and charging <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">PM E-DRIVE</button>

hs.b: • Vehicle-to-grid: EVs send power back to the grid → owner earns, battery lasts longer, helps meet peak demand

• 2024, replaced FAME-II: subsidies for EVs and charging
  • PM e-Bus Sewa (38,000+ buses) + 5% GST on EVs

cm.0: India Electric Mobility Index: NITI Aayog + WRI India ranking of states on EV adoption, charging readiness and EV research; 1st edition Aug 2025, 2nd Sep 2026 (Delhi top both times).
cm.1: Inverted GST = parts (batteries, components) are taxed at 18% but the finished EV only at 5%, so makers can't recover the extra tax paid.
cm.2: Vehicle-to-grid = parked EVs feed power back to the grid at peak times.
cm.3: FAME-II = the earlier EV subsidy scheme (2019–24), replaced by PM E-DRIVE.

topics.name: DM spine

rows.t: India is multi-hazard: 59% of land quake-prone + 12% (40 million ha) flood-prone + 5,700 of 7,500 km coast exposed to cyclones and tsunamis + 68% of farmland drought-prone + 5.4 million displaced in 2024 (IDMC)
building codes poorly enforced + expert warnings ignored (Joshimath: Mishra Committee warned in 1976)
flash floods and cloudbursts hard to forecast, no local warning (Dharali, Uttarkashi 2025)
the hazard itself + climate change makes extremes more frequent
lakes and floodplains encroached (Chennai 2015) communities, and forest and tribals specially vulnerable (assam floods)
building on unstable slopes + deforestation + mining + hydel projects (Himachal 2023)
insurance covers only ≈3.7%, most losses uninsured
agencies poorly coordinated (Kerala 2018 dam releases, Kedarnath 2013)

Health: deaths and injuries · Environment: ecosystems wrecked · Economy: losses doubled in 20 years (GAR 2025) · Governance: providing relief burden on states · Society: poor, women, disabled hit hardest
retrofit schools and hospitals first + safe infrastructure (CDRI) · $1 on DRR saves $15 (GAR 2025)
disaster lessons in NCERT Classes 8–10 + mock drills (Exercise Suraksha Chakra 2025: 55 sites, 18 districts in NCR)
hazard maps + Disaster Risk Index for sharing funds
disaster funds + risk transfer <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">Disaster finance</button><button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">Insurance</button>

response: NDRF (16 battalions) + Incident Response System + ERSS-112 + golden hour (Silkyara 2023: 41 rescued after 17 days) · recovery: post-disaster needs assessment + build back better (Bhuj 2001: owner-driven rebuilding)
<button class="hs" data-h="3">early warning</button> to the last mile (Pacific tsunami warning costs ≈4 million dollars a year vs ≈8 billion dollars of aid after 2004)
inter-agency coordination: National Executive Committee + Incident Response Teams + CDRI abroad
capacity building: Aapda Mitra volunteers + tech tools + IUINDRR-NIDM network of 330+ universities

hs.b:
• Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure (lower with more capacity) · hazard = event that can harm → disaster = when it overwhelms a community's capacity to cope
  • Vulnerability, 4 types: physical (weak houses on slopes) + social (age, gender, caste, disability) + economic (poverty, no insurance) + environmental (degraded ecosystems)
  • Exposure: people and assets in the hazard zone (Joshimath 2023: town on old landslide debris)
  • Cascading risk: one hazard sets off another (Chamoli 2021: rock-ice avalanche → flood → Tapovan tunnel · Sikkim 2023: GLOF → Chungthang dam breach)

• 16th FC: ₹2.04 lakh crore for SDRF + SDMF (2026–31), up 27% + heatwaves and lightning added to notified disasters
  • SDRF 75:25 (90:10 Himalayan and NE) · NDRF 100% Centre, for "severe" calamities · NDMF/SDMF for mitigation
  • Issues: one-size Disaster Risk Index misses hilly and coastal states + "severe" undefined + ₹4 lakh per death unchanged for a decade + index weights: hazard 70, vulnerability 30
  • Fix: blended finance + debt-for-resilience swaps + review the index every 5 years

• Only ≈1% protection; most disaster losses uninsured
  • Worked: Nagaland (2024), first state with parametric insurance (auto-payout when rain crosses a threshold) · Mixed: PMFBY (late claims, states left in 2020)
  • India: Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act (Dec 2025) + "Insurance for All by 2047" (IRDAI) + GST on insurance cut to 0%

• SACHET (Common Alerting Protocol) + cell-broadcast alerts in local languages
  • Mission Mausam (2024, ₹2,000 crore): 50 Doppler radars + AI forecasts · Bharat Forecast System: 6 km grid, village-level nowcasts
  • Worked: INCOIS tsunami centre (alerts in minutes) · Failed: Dharali 2025 (no local warning)
  • UN Early Warnings for All by 2027

• Risk tools: Web-DCRA, Flood Hazard Atlas, Glacial Lake Dataset
  • Warnings: SACHET, Damini (lightning), Mausam app, NCRMP for coastal states + Odisha's SATARK platform
  • HADR abroad: Operation Dost (Türkiye, Syria) + Operation Brahma (Myanmar 2025)
  • Worked: Wayanad 2024 (Army built a 190-ft Bailey bridge in ≈1.5 days)

cm.0: IDMC = Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, a Geneva body that counts people forced from homes inside their own country.
cm.1: Exposure = how many people and how much property sit in the hazard's path. Same quake, empty desert = low exposure; crowded city = high.
cm.2: Cascading risk = one disaster triggers the next, like dominoes (avalanche → flood → dam breach).
cm.3: Mishra Committee (1976) = panel that warned Joshimath sits on old landslide debris and asked for curbs on heavy construction; ignored.
cm.4: GAR = UN Global Assessment Report on Disaster Risk Reduction (by UNDRR), published every few years.
cm.5: CDRI = Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure: India-led global body (2019) helping countries build roads, power and hospitals that survive disasters.
cm.6: Exercise Suraksha Chakra = large mock drill for an earthquake in Delhi-NCR (2025) run by NDMA with the Army.
cm.7: Disaster Risk Index = a score for each state's hazard + exposure + vulnerability; the Finance Commission uses it to share disaster funds.
cm.8: SDRF = State Disaster Response Fund (money for relief after a disaster); SDMF = State Disaster Mitigation Fund (money to cut risk before one). NDRF / NDMF = the national versions.
cm.9: Here NDRF = National Disaster Response Fund (DM Act, s.46), not the National Disaster Response Force.
cm.10: Debt-for-resilience swap = a lender forgives part of a country's debt if the money saved is spent on disaster-proofing.
cm.11: Parametric insurance = pays out automatically when a measured trigger is crossed (rain above X mm, wind above Y km/h), no loss survey needed.
cm.12: PMFBY = Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, crop insurance for farmers at low premiums.
cm.13: Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act (Dec 2025) = insurance law amendment allowing 100% FDI in insurers and easing rules to widen cover.
cm.14: IRDAI = Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, the insurance regulator.
cm.15: NDRF here = National Disaster Response Force, the specialist rescue force. Don't mix it up with the NDRF fund (National Disaster Response Fund).
cm.16: Incident Response System = a fixed chain of command at a disaster site: who leads, who handles operations, logistics and planning, so nobody waits for orders.
cm.17: ERSS-112 = Emergency Response Support System: one number, 112, for police, fire, ambulance. Golden hour = the first hour or so after a disaster, when rescue saves the most lives.
cm.18: PDNA (post-disaster needs assessment) = a survey after a disaster of damage, losses and what it will cost to rebuild.
cm.19: SACHET / Common Alerting Protocol = one standard format for disaster alerts so the same warning goes out on SMS, TV, radio and apps at once.
cm.20: Cell broadcast = an alert pushed to every phone in an area at once, even without the number on a list.
cm.21: Mission Mausam (2024) = IMD programme to make India weather-ready: more radars, supercomputers, AI forecasts.
cm.22: Nowcast = a forecast for the next few hours, very local (thunderstorm in the next 3 hours over this block).
cm.23: INCOIS = Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Hyderabad; runs India's tsunami warning centre.
cm.24: Aapda Mitra = NDMA scheme training local volunteers in first response (search, rescue, first aid) in disaster-prone districts.
cm.25: IUINDRR-NIDM = Indian Universities and Institutions Network for Disaster Risk Reduction, run by NIDM: links 330+ universities for disaster research and teaching.
cm.26: Web-DCRA = web-based Dynamic Composite Risk Atlas: NDMA's online risk map that combines hazards, people and assets.
cm.27: SATARK = Odisha's web platform (OSDMA) that sends warnings for many hazards (lightning, heat, floods, drought) to officials and people.
cm.28: HADR = Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief: armed forces sent abroad after a disaster (rescue teams, field hospitals, supplies).
cm.29: Operation Dost = India's rescue and relief mission after the Türkiye–Syria earthquake (2023).
cm.30: Bailey bridge = a prefabricated steel bridge the Army can assemble quickly by hand.

topics.name: India's DM framework

rows.t: DM = planned, coordinated effort to reduce risk, build resilience and protect lives and livelihoods
Shift: relief-centric → zero-casualty, proactive <button class="hs chipx" data-h="0">Reactive → proactive</button>
The law <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">DM Act 2005</button><button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">DM Amendment Act 2025</button><button class="hs chipx" data-h="3">NDMP 2019</button>
Global frameworks <button class="hs chipx" data-h="4">Sendai vs Hyogo</button><button class="hs chipx" data-h="5">Resilience</button>
Local level <button class="hs chipx" data-h="6">Community DRR</button>
"severe calamity" undefined + sector laws scattered (EPA 1986, Factories Act 1948, Epidemic Diseases Act 1897) + no fixed liability for officials
disaster databases only from 2025
member vacancies + many states still relief-heavy
mitigation money under-used (CAG)

Enforce the 2025 amendments + DRR in every development plan + social audits of relief + regular Parliament review of NDMA + courts enforce duties (SC, Gaurav Kumar Bansal 2021: ex gratia for COVID deaths)

hs.b:
• Relief after the event → risk reduction before it: DM Act 2005 covers the whole cycle
  • NDMP 2019 + DM Amendment Act 2025 + 16th FC disaster funds + Mission Mausam
  • Worked: Odisha, Phailin 2013 (≈10 lakh evacuated, ≈44 deaths vs ≈10,000 in the 1999 super cyclone)
  • Sendai + Paris + SDGs (all 2015) read together: NDMP aligns all three

• 3 tiers: NDMA (PM) → SDMA (CM) → DDMA (Collector) + National Executive Committee (Home Secretary)
  • NDRF (force) + NIDM (training) + plans mandatory at every level + NDRF/SDRF funds
  • Used: COVID-19 lockdown (first nationwide use) · Failed: Uttarakhand 2013 (state authority had barely met)

• Urban DM Authorities in every municipal corporation (except Delhi, Chandigarh), headed by the Commissioner
  • National and state disaster databases + NDMA sets minimum relief standards and audits plans + SDRF in every state
  • Gaps: NDMA still under MHA + member vacancies + vague urban plans

• Aligns with Sendai, SDGs, Paris + PM's 10-point agenda; first plan 2016
  • Themes: understanding risk + inter-agency coordination + risk governance + capacity development + preparedness and response + recovery
  • Goals for 2022, 2027, 2030 + risk matrices for 20+ hazards + nodal ministry for each
  • Worked: Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan 2013 · Cyclone Fani 2019 (SOPs, NDRF pre-positioned)

• Sendai 2015–30, 7 targets: reduce deaths + people affected + economic loss + infrastructure damage · increase DRR strategies (by 2020) + international support + early warning access
  • 4 priorities: understand risk + strengthen risk governance + invest in DRR + preparedness and build back better
  • Hyogo 2005–15 (5 priorities) managed disasters; Sendai manages risk: prevention over response + DRR in every sector + local ownership
  • India before Sendai: DM Act 2005, NDMA, NDRF · after: NDMP 2016/2019, 10-point agenda, CDRI 2019

• Anticipate + absorb + adapt + recover, and "bounce forward" (build back better)
  • Measured by: early warning and risk info (anticipate) + strong infrastructure and safety nets (absorb) + flexible institutions (adapt) + fast, inclusive rebuilding (recover)
  • Worked: Odisha, Fani 2019 (≈12 lakh evacuated, ≈64 deaths) · Failed: Chennai 2015 (lakes built over)

• National Project for Community-Based DRR in PRIs (₹507 crore, MoPR + NDMA): 20 states, 81 districts
  • Pozhuthana panchayat, Kerala 2018 (risk maps, village response teams) + Tampara wetland, Odisha (eco-DRR)
  • Aapda Mitra + SACHET alerts

cm.0: National Executive Committee = NDMA's working arm, chaired by the Union Home Secretary; turns NDMA policy into action.
cm.1: NIDM = National Institute of Disaster Management: trains officials and does DM research.
cm.2: PM's 10-point agenda (2016) = India's DRR priorities: DRR in all development, risk cover for all, women's leadership, risk mapping, tech, local capacity, etc.
cm.3: Build back better = rebuild stronger and safer than before, not just as it was.
cm.4: Hyogo Framework (2005–15) = earlier UN DRR plan, focused on managing disasters; replaced by Sendai (2015–30), which focuses on managing risk.
cm.5: Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 = colonial law letting governments take special measures in epidemics (used in COVID-19).

topics.name: Earthquakes

rows.t: 59% of land in Zones II–V (IS 1893:2016) · BIS 2025 code added Zone VI, withdrawn Mar 2026 → 2016 code back
building codes not enforced + most houses non-engineered
earthquake early warning only a pilot (Uttarakhand)
Indian plate pushing into Eurasia (Himalaya, NE) + intraplate stress (Latur 1993)
low awareness, little drill culture
dense cities on soft soil + reservoir-induced quakes (dams, mining)
buildings kill, not the shaking + liquefaction, landslides, tsunamis + roads, power, hospitals cut
NDMA guideline
retrofit schools and hospitals first
drills (Exercise Suraksha Chakra 2025, NCR)
Earthquake Disaster Risk Index for 50 cities
seismic observatories 80 (2014) → 168 (2025) + BhooKamp and India Quake apps
NDRF: 16 battalions, 1,149 personnel each
Cases <button class="hs chipx" data-h="1">Major earthquakes</button>

hs.b:
• Earthquake-resistant new construction + selective retrofitting of schools and hospitals
  • Enforce codes (IS 1893, National Building Code) + Incident Command System and Emergency Operations Centres
  • National Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project + National Centre for Seismology

• Latur 1993 (≈10,000 dead, on the "stable" Deccan plate)
  • Bhuj 2001 (M7.7, ≈20,000 dead) → Gujarat rebuilt with GSDMA + owner-driven reconstruction (worked)
  • Kashmir 2005 (M7.6) · Sikkim 2011 (M6.9) · Nepal 2015 (M7.8, Bihar hit) · Imphal 2016 (M6.7)
  • World: Pacific Ring of Fire (≈90% of earthquakes, ≈75% of active volcanoes) → Kamchatka M8.8 (2025) sent tsunami waves to Russia and Japan

cm.0: IS 1893 = BIS code that maps India into seismic zones (II = low to V = highest) and sets how buildings must resist quakes.
cm.1: Reservoir-induced quake = the weight and water pressure of a big dam's lake triggers quakes (Koyna 1967).
cm.2: Liquefaction = during shaking, wet sandy soil loses strength and behaves like liquid, so buildings sink or tilt.
cm.3: National Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project: NDMA plan for safer buildings (codes, retrofitting, training engineers and masons). National Centre for Seismology (MoES): records every quake and issues alerts.
cm.4: GSDMA = Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, set up after Bhuj 2001.

topics.name: Tsunamis

rows.t: 13 tsunamis in the Indian Ocean in 300 years; 2004 the most destructive to hit India
undersea megathrust quakes (2004: M9.1 Sumatra–Andaman, Indian plate under Burma plate) + submarine landslides, volcanic collapse
building in coastal no-development zones + mangroves cleared
2004: ≈2.3 lakh dead in 14 countries, India ≈10,700 (Nagapattinam, A&N worst) + boats, harbours, fishing livelihoods lost + farmland salinised + tourism hit
NDMA guideline
mangrove bio-shields (Pichavaram reduced 2004 damage) + CRZ no-development zones
regular coastal drills
Indian Tsunami Early Warning System (INCOIS, Hyderabad, 2007): detects Indian Ocean quakes in under 10 minutes + last-mile alerts (SACHET)

hs.b:
• Inundation and hazard maps + monitoring networks
  • Bio-shields (mangroves, shelterbelts) + built barriers + safe coastal construction (CRZ)
  • Coastal drills + capacity building

cm.0: Megathrust quake = the biggest kind of quake, where one tectonic plate slides under another along a huge fault.
cm.1: Bio-shield = a belt of mangroves or coastal trees that breaks the force of waves and wind.

rows.t: 12% of land (40 million ha) flood-prone + 85% of the 1,200 mm rain falls in 3–4 months
no city flood plan + 52% of towns have no master plan
extreme rain, cyclones, snowmelt
drains and wetlands encroached (Mumbai's Mithi river)
concrete stops infiltration + deforestation, siltation + embankment breaches
city own revenue only ≈1% of GDP
deaths, homes and crops lost + water-borne disease + transport and power cut
NDMA guideline
flood-plain zoning + sponge cities
Flood Hazard Atlas + Climate Smart Cities Assessment Framework
C-FLOOD forecasting
devolve urban planning to ULBs (74th Amendment)
<button class="hs" data-h="1">Urban floods</button>

hs.b:
• Structural: reservoirs, embankments, desilting, catchment treatment
  • Non-structural: flood-plain zoning, flood forecasting, community preparedness (Aapda Mitra)
  • Urban Flood Guidelines 2010 + AMRUT stormwater drains + sponge-city ideas

• Mumbai, 26 July 2005: ≈944 mm in 24 hours + Mithi river encroached + drains built for 25 mm/hour → ≈1,000 dead
  • Chennai, Dec 2015: extreme rain + sudden release from Chembarambakkam lake + lakes and Adyar floodplain built over → ≈340+ dead
  • Urban flood risk 3.6–7x by 2070 (World Bank) + urban people 480 million (2020) → 951 million (2050)

cm.0: Climate Smart Cities Assessment Framework (MoHUA, 2019): scores cities on climate readiness, incl. flood and water management, green cover, energy and mobility.
cm.1: C-FLOOD = a web platform (CWC + C-DAC) giving village-level flood inundation forecasts up to 2 days ahead. 74th Amendment (next line) = gave urban local bodies constitutional status and listed their functions (12th Schedule).

topics.name: Landslides

rows.t: 12.6–15% of land (0.42 million sq km): Himalaya, Western Ghats, NE hills, Nilgiris
building on steep slopes unregulated (Aizawl, Sikkim)
intense rain + quakes + weak geology (Western Ghats: basalt + steep slopes)
slopes levelled for farming (Malin 2014)
road cutting, deforestation, mining, blasting, hydel projects
homes buried + roads, power, hydel cut + debris dams rivers → flash floods downstream
NDMA guideline
retaining walls, bunds, terrace farming, afforestation
hazard <button class="hs" data-h="1">zonation mapping</button>
slope sensors + rain-threshold warnings
Related <button class="hs chipx" data-h="2">Land subsidence</button>
Cases: Wayanad, 30 July 2024 (200+ dead) · Malin, Pune 2014 (≈150, slopes levelled for farming) · Joshimath 2023

hs.b:
• No construction on slopes of 30° or more + settlements and roads kept out of high-risk zones, farming in valleys
  • National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019): hazard mapping (GSI) + monitoring and early warning + awareness + capacity building + mountain zone rules + stabilisation (Landslide Risk Mitigation Scheme)
  • Bhusanket portal + landslide insurance

• Divide hill terrain into zones by how likely landslides are
  • Inputs: slope + geology + soil + drainage + land use + rainfall + past landslides; made with GIS, satellites, field checks
  • Scales: 1:50,000 (GSI national) → 1:10,000 (town planning) → site level
  • Use: where not to build + road and dam alignment + where to put early warning sensors

• Ground sinks as soil or rock below is compressed: groundwater pumping + mining + building
  • Delhi worst (51 mm a year, 2,000+ buildings at risk) + Joshimath, Mussoorie
